title: The Room of the Bell House
premise: Pest controller Isandro Zhou is summoned to Bell House, a frostbound farmhouse where the infestation leaves fingerprints in dust and answers questions asked aloud. His habit of documenting everything—recordings, logs, prayers of proof—becomes the only thing keeping him anchored when he realizes the house's sleep recordings contain a second voice, one that has been answering him in his own cadence for years. As the frost spreads into patterns that mirror his mother's handwriting, Isandro learns the house survives by trading identities: it keeps whoever sings the song's last verse. In the end, Isandro refuses to sing, instead feeding the house a documented confession of its own history, and walks out at dawn while the previous owner—the voice on the tapes—takes his place inside.
about_author: Emrys Vane is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent a decade crawling through basements no one else would enter. They write horror about people whose jobs require them to look closely at things that would rather not be seen.

chapters.title: Call-Out
chapters.summary: Isandro Zhou takes a pest control job at Bell House after three contractors quit; the client, Mrs. Aldous, pays triple and asks only that he work alone. He finds droppings arranged in neat rows and fingerprints pressed into dust on the ceiling. POV: Isandro. Emotional beat: professional curiosity curdling into unease as his documentation instinct kicks in like a reflex prayer.

chapters.title: What the Dust Keeps
chapters.summary: Isandro maps the house room by room, logging anomalies: cold spots that follow him, a nursery with fresh handprints too large to be a child's. He sets cameras and audio recorders per protocol. POV: Isandro. Emotional beat: the comfort of procedure, the belief that anything written down can be survived, tested by a hallway that appears longer on his return trips.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: Reviewing overnight recordings, Isandro hears himself talking in his sleep—and a second voice answering questions he never asked aloud. The voice knows his mother's name. He checks the house's old tape archive and finds decades of identical recordings from previous occupants. POV: Isandro. Emotional beat: dread shifting from the house to what it knows about him personally.

chapters.title: Mrs. Aldous's Ledger
chapters.summary: Isandro confronts the client, who reveals she is not the owner but the caretaker, bound by contract since 1974. She shows him a ledger of every worker who entered; each name is followed by a date of death or a word: 'kept.' Her own entry has no ending yet. POV: alternating Isandro and Mrs. Aldous. Emotional beat: complicity—she warns him because warning is her only remaining freedom.

chapters.title: Frost Script
chapters.summary: Overnight frost forms words on the windows in handwriting Isandro recognizes as his dead mother's. The messages are mundane, loving, wrong. He documents them obsessively until he notices the script is practicing—each night closer to fluency, learning to be her. POV: Isandro. Emotional beat: grief weaponized; the horror of wanting to believe the windows.

chapters.title: The Song
chapters.summary: The audio captures a lullaby threaded through the second voice's answers—a verse-and-refrain structure missing its final verse. Mrs. Aldous explains the rule: the house keeps whoever completes the song. Every 'kept' occupant got one verse further before stopping. POV: Mrs. Aldous, with Isandro's recordings interleaved. Emotional beat: loyalty vs. truth—she begs him to leave; he stays because leaving means abandoning the evidence, and the evidence is starting to feel like company.

chapters.title: Invisible No Longer
chapters.summary: The house stops pretending. Doors open onto rooms from Isandro's childhood; the fingerprints match his own. He realizes staying invisible was never an option—the house selected him months ago through the job listing itself. His documentation now reads like a courtship transcript. POV: Isandro. Emotional beat: the collapse of his core belief that observation protects you; being watched back.

chapters.title: Verse Fourteen
chapters.summary: Sleep-deprived, Isandro catches himself humming the refrain and finds fourteen verses written in frost on his own notebook pages—in his handwriting, which he doesn't remember writing. One verse remains. The second voice pleads through the speakers: it was a person once, and finishing the song will free them both. POV: Isandro. Emotional beat: temptation at its most reasonable; the price of survival offered as mercy.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Climax. On the coldest night, the house sings verses one through fourteen in his mother's voice, waiting. Isandro instead reads aloud his complete documentation—the house's own history, extracted from the ledger and tapes: names, dates, the original owner's bargain made during a famine winter. Naming it, he refuses to sing along. The frost shatters inward. POV: Isandro. Emotional beat: truth as exorcism; loyalty redirected from the house to the kept.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Dawn. Mrs. Aldous finds the door unlocked for the first time in fifty years; inside, the second voice weeps with relief as the house accepts it as final tenant, its identity finally its own. Isandro files his report, stamps it closed, and drives away—but at a red light hums four notes before catching himself. POV: Mrs. Aldous closing, then Isandro. Emotional beat: survival achieved at cost; some songs stay in the blood.
